summary: Describes a mechanism for FTP clients and servers to implement security and authentication using TLS, with the FTP security extensions from RFC 2228. It covers the required subset and parameters. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC specifies how FTP clients and servers negotiate TLS protection. It distinguishes the command connection from the separate connections that carry file data, so each can have its own protection setting.

questions: how to secure ftp with tls
what does auth tls do in ftp
what is prot p in ftp
what is the ccc command in ftp
subtitle: How FTP clients and servers use TLS to protect the control session and, separately, file transfers.

tldr.problem: FTP security extensions did not specify exactly how clients and servers should use TLS, leaving room for incompatible behavior.
tldr.mechanism: The client requests TLS with AUTH TLS, then sends PBSZ 0 and PROT to choose data-connection protection. CCC can return the control connection to plaintext.
tldr.outcome: The commands let peers negotiate protection without requiring every session to use the same policy. RFC 4217 is updated by RFC 8996.

today: RFC 4217 is a Proposed Standard, published in October 2005, and is updated by RFC 8996. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: TLS for FTP Sessions
sections.content:
RFC 4217 combines FTP, the FTP security extensions, and TLS. It defines how FTP uses AUTH, PBSZ, PROT, and CCC to negotiate authentication, integrity, and confidentiality.

A session begins on the normal FTP control port without protection. AUTH can start TLS, while PBSZ and PROT set the protection for later data connections. These commands provide negotiation tools; they do not guarantee that every session or transfer is protected.
sections.plainLanguage: FTP uses one connection for commands and separate connections for data. This RFC explains how to negotiate TLS on each connection type.

sections.title: Starting TLS with AUTH
sections.content:
A client that wants a protected session SHOULD send AUTH TLS. A server that accepts it replies 234 and begins TLS negotiation. The server SHOULD accept TLS-C as a synonym, but a 334 response is incorrect because this procedure does not use an ADAT exchange.

The client MUST still send USER after TLS negotiation, even if TLS supplied authentication information. AUTH also resets transfer parameters, including the user identity, default data ports, transfer type, structure, mode, and working directory. A server may refuse commands until the session reaches its required protection level.
sections.plainLanguage: The client asks for TLS with AUTH TLS, and the server accepts with reply 234. The client still identifies its FTP user after the TLS negotiation.

sections.title: Setting Data-Connection Protection
sections.content:
AUTH protects the control connection only. To protect data connections, the client MUST send PBSZ and then PROT after TLS succeeds. For TLS, PBSZ MUST have the value 0, and PROT uses C for Clear or P for Private.

The initial data-connection setting is Clear. With Private, the client and server negotiate TLS on each data connection before transferring data. After a server accepts a PROT setting with reply 200, it applies to later data connections until another accepted PROT, REIN, or a new AUTH negotiation changes the state.
sections.plainLanguage: Protecting FTP commands does not automatically protect file data. PBSZ 0 and PROT P request TLS on data connections; PROT C leaves them unprotected.

sections.title: Returning the Control Connection to Plaintext
sections.content:
CCC asks the server to end TLS on the control connection while leaving the socket open. The server replies 500 if it does not support CCC, 533 if the connection is not protected, and 534 if it declines at that time. If accepted, it replies 200 and expects later commands in plaintext.

After CCC, the server accepts no more PBSZ or PROT commands. Existing data-connection protection settings remain in effect. The RFC warns that CCC has serious security issues and says clients should not assume a server will allow it.
sections.plainLanguage: CCC can turn the command connection back to plaintext while leaving the current data setting in place. Clearing that connection creates security risks, so a server may refuse.

sections.title: Policy and Failed Negotiations
sections.content:
A server may require TLS before accepting some commands, choose which TLS settings are allowed, or require protection for data transfers. It SHOULD check the PROT setting when the client requests a transfer rather than when it sends PORT or PASV.

Reply 521 indicates that the data connection cannot open with the selected PROT setting. Reply 522 indicates that TLS on the data connection failed or was unacceptable. If the control TLS negotiation fails during its handshake, the connection is in an unknown state and should be dropped.
sections.plainLanguage: The server can apply its own protection policy. FTP reply codes tell the client when a data connection has the wrong setting or its TLS negotiation failed.

sections.title: Checking the Identities at Both Ends
sections.content:
The RFC discusses X.509 certificates as TLS authentication tokens. It strongly recommends using the same server certificate on the control and data connections, or another method that lets the client compare their identities. Without server certificates, protection against a man-in-the-middle attack is limited.

Using the same client certificate on control and data connections is also strongly recommended. Without strong client authentication, a malicious client may still hijack a data connection. CCC can weaken protection by returning the control connection to plaintext.
sections.plainLanguage: TLS protection depends on checking who is on the other end. Matching identities across the control and data connections helps prevent one connection from being taken over.
